title: Erdős Problem #78: Constructive Ramsey Lower Bound
description: Give a constructive proof that R(k) > C^k. Equivalently, build explicit graphs with no clique/independent set of size c·log n. Best: Li (2023) achieves (log n)^C. Open ($100).

meta.assumptions: 1 axiom: ramseyNumber. Structure fields are object definitions, not assumptions.

sections.title: Header and Imports
sections.summary: Documentation header with problem statement, historical results (Erdős 1947, Cohen 2015, Li 2023), $100 prize, and imports for Mathlib's Tactic, Nat.Basic, Finset.Basic, and SimpleGraph.Basic.

sections.title: Graph Definitions
sections.summary: Custom SimpleG structure with adjacency, symmetry, irreflexivity. Defines hasClique and hasIndepSet via Finset subsets. Axiomatizes ramseyNumber and its specification.

sections.title: Probabilistic Lower Bound
sections.summary: Erdős 1947 probabilistic bound: R(k) ≥ C^k for some C > 1 (axiomatized). Asymptotic √2 bound axiomatized separately with ε-approximation.

sections.title: Constructive Results
sections.summary: IsExplicit predicate (axiomatized as True). Cohen (2015): 2^{(log log n)^C}. Li (2023): (log n)^C. Both axiomatized with Real.exp and Real.log formulations.

sections.title: Main Open Problem
sections.summary: The $100 challenge: construct explicit n-vertex graphs with α(G), ω(G) < c·log n. Axiomatized as the existence of c > 0 with explicit graph family.

sections.title: Upper Bounds
sections.summary: Erdős–Szekeres R(k) ≤ 4^k (1935) and CGMS R(k) ≤ (4-ε)^k (2023), both axiomatized.

overview.historicalContext: Erdős's 1947 probabilistic proof that $R(k) > k \cdot 2^{k/2}/e$ was the birth of the probabilistic method in combinatorics — one of the most influential proof techniques of the 20th century. The proof shows that a random 2-coloring of $K_n$'s edges has no monochromatic $K_k$ with positive probability when $n < \sqrt{2}^k$, but it gives no explicit coloring. Erdős offered $\$100$ for a constructive matching bound. Despite 75+ years of effort, the gap remains enormous. The best explicit constructions were Paley graphs (1933), achieving $\alpha(G), \omega(G) \sim \sqrt{n}$ via quadratic residues and the Weil bound — an exponential gap from the target $c \cdot \log n$. Cohen (2015) achieved $2^{(\log \log n)^C}$ using algebraic geometry, and Li (2023) improved to $(\log n)^C$, the current state of the art. Meanwhile, the upper bound was dramatically improved: the $4^k$ barrier from Erdős–Szekeres (1935) stood for 88 years until Campos, Griffiths, Morris, and Sahasrabudhe (2023) proved $R(k) \le (4 - \varepsilon)^k$.
overview.problemStatement: Give a constructive (explicit, polynomial-time) proof that $R(k) > C^k$ for some $C > 1$. Equivalently, construct explicit $n$-vertex graphs with no clique or independent set of size $\ge c \cdot \log n$. Prize: $\$100$.
overview.text: Give a constructive proof that R(k) > C^k. Equivalently, build explicit graphs with no clique/independent set of size c·log n. Best: Li (2023) achieves (log n)^C. Open ($100).
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization defines a custom `SimpleG n` structure, `hasClique`, `hasIndepSet`, and axiomatizes the diagonal Ramsey number $R(k)$. The probabilistic lower bound ($R(k) \ge C^k$), constructive results (Cohen 2015, Li 2023), the main open problem, and upper bounds (Erdős–Szekeres 1935, CGMS 2023) are all axiomatized. The `IsExplicit` predicate is defined as `True` since constructibility is a meta-property not expressible in Lean's type system.
keyInsights: The probabilistic method gives $R(k) \ge \sqrt{2}^k$ but is inherently non-constructive — this is one of the deepest gaps between existence and construction in mathematics

Paley graphs ($\alpha, \omega \sim \sqrt{n}$) vs. target ($c \cdot \log n$) represents an exponential gap: $e^{\sqrt{\log n}}$ vs. $e^{c'}$ — the largest known constructive-vs-probabilistic gap in combinatorics
Li's (2023) $(\log n)^C$ bound is the best known, but the gap from polynomial-in-$\log n$ to linear-in-$\log n$ remains fundamental
CGMS (2023) broke the 88-year $4^k$ upper bound barrier, proving $R(k) \le (4-\varepsilon)^k$ — current best bounds: $(\sqrt{2})^k \lesssim R(k) \lesssim (4-\varepsilon)^k$
The formalization axiomatizes `IsExplicit` as `True` since polynomial-time computability is a meta-property not capturable in Lean's logic
A constructive proof would have profound implications for derandomization, complexity theory (P vs BPP), and the foundations of the probabilistic method

conclusion.summary: Erdős Problem #78 ($100 prize) remains one of the most famous open problems in combinatorics. The formalization captures the 108-line Lean 4 axiomatization of Ramsey numbers, the probabilistic lower bound, constructive results (Cohen 2015, Li 2023), and upper bounds (Erdős–Szekeres 1935, CGMS 2023). The file has 0 sorries — all statements are axiomatized rather than proved.
conclusion.implications: A constructive proof would bridge the gap between probabilistic existence and explicit construction, with major implications for pseudorandomness, circuit complexity, and derandomization. It would show that the probabilistic method, while powerful, is not fundamentally stronger than deterministic arguments for Ramsey-type problems.
openQuestions: Can explicit graphs achieve independence number O(log n), matching the probabilistic bound?
Is the probabilistic method inherently stronger than explicit constructions for Ramsey numbers?
What is the true base C in R(k) ~ C^k? Current bounds: √2 ≤ C ≤ 4-ε
Can algebraic or number-theoretic constructions (beyond Paley graphs) close the gap?
Does P = BPP imply constructive Ramsey bounds, or are they independent?

references: Ramsey (1930): original theorem on monochromatic subsets
Erdős–Szekeres (1935): R(k) ≤ C(2k-2, k-1) < 4^k via recurrence
Erdős (1947): R(k) > k·2^{k/2}/e, birth of the probabilistic method
Paley (1933): Paley graphs achieve clique/independence number √n
Cohen (2015): explicit graph, no clique/indep set 2^{(log log n)^C}
Li (2023): improved to (log n)^C, current state of the art
